learningSection.title: Why these wallets fail, and why they will keep failing?
learningSection.body: Your Bitcoin is safe when you have the right knowledge, not when you buy a device. Bitcoin already has the tools, you just need to learn how to use them.

offering.title: Plans

PremiumPage.metadataTitle: Become an expert — 1:1 Bitcoin self-custody mentorship
PremiumPage.metadataDescription: One-to-one sessions to design, build and verify your own Bitcoin self-custody setup, at a convenient price.
PremiumPage.title: Be an expert for a convenient price
PremiumPage.subtitle: The knowledge is free; the difference is having someone who sits with you, reviews your hardware and walks you through your first transaction — until you can verify it yourself.

setup.title: Designing your setup
setup.body: Which hardware, how many keys, one device or a multisig — chosen against your threat model, not a sales page.

keys.title: Generating and storing keys
keys.body: Dice, entropy, backups, passphrases and metal. We do it once, together, and you write it down in a way you can actually recover.

verify.title: Verifying instead of trusting
verify.body: You build and sign a real transaction, then check it with your own node and your own eyes.

support.title: Keep asking
support.body: A subscription keeps the conversation open while your setup, the firmware or the threats change.

PremiumPage.architecturesTitle: Want to explore on your own?

FirmwareDiagram.model: threat model — what malicious firmware could reach
FirmwareDiagram.prompt: Select any element to see its full name and what malicious firmware could do with it.
FirmwareDiagram.caption: Simplified threat model of the Trezor Safe 5: if the signed firmware image itself were malicious, these are the parts of the device it could lie about or abuse. The secure element is shown because firmware might try to attack it — not because it is easy to infect.

display.name: Touchscreen display
display.description: Shows an address, amount or fee that differs from the transaction it actually signs.

touch.name: Touch confirmation
touch.description: Registers a tap you never made, so a payout looks approved on the spot.

usb.name: USB data link
usb.description: Tells Trezor Suite the balance and recipient it expects while sending something else to the chip.

seed.name: Seed and private keys
seed.description: Reads the decrypted seed from device memory and signs transactions of its own.

passphrase.name: Passphrase entry
passphrase.description: Captures the passphrase as it is typed and clones every hidden wallet it unlocks.

storage.name: Firmware storage
storage.description: Rewrites its own image and re-infects the device after a factory reset.

secure-element.name: Secure element
secure-element.description: Replays PIN attempts past the limit and hides the counters that would expose it.

randomness.name: Random number generator
randomness.description: Feeds rigged entropy, so keys generated after infection can be guessed.

HardwareWalletDiagram.model: threat model — every component malicious firmware sits in front of, today and on future models
HardwareWalletDiagram.prompt: Select any element to see its full name and what malicious firmware could do with it.
HardwareWalletDiagram.caption: Generic threat model for commercial hardware wallets: the firmware sits between the user and every component, so a malicious image can lie about, capture or reroute whatever passes through it. Wireless links, cameras, biometrics and battery or tamper circuitry are arriving on newer models — the exposure begins the moment the component ships.

display.name: Screen
display.description: Draws an address, amount or fee that differs from the transaction the user actually approved.

input.name: Touchscreen and buttons
input.description: Registers taps and presses that never happened, and captures the PIN on the way in.

usb.name: USB data link
usb.description: Tells the desktop app one transaction while handing a different one to the signing routine.

wireless.name: Wireless link (NFC or Bluetooth)
wireless.description: Opens a channel to a nearby attacker that the screen never shows — standard on newer models.

camera.name: Camera and QR scanner
camera.description: Reads or rewrites the QR payload so an air-gapped scan signs something other than what was shown.

storage-media.name: Removable storage
storage-media.description: Swaps the transaction file on the card for one the user never reviewed.

seed.name: Seed and key storage
seed.description: Reads the decrypted seed from device memory and signs transactions of its own.

secure-element.name: Secure element
secure-element.description: Replays PIN attempts past the limit, fakes a verification result, or hides the counters that would expose it.

biometrics.name: Fingerprint sensor
biometrics.description: Replays an earlier scan or reports a match for a finger that was never placed.

power.name: Battery, charging and tamper mesh
power.description: Suppresses tamper and battery alerts, or browns out the chip so a check is skipped.

WalletKnowledge.metadataTitle: Wallet architectures — how popular wallets are built
WalletKnowledge.metadataDescription: A knowledge base of Bitcoin wallet architectures: how each brand is built, where its keys live, and how it has failed in public.
WalletKnowledge.title: Wallet architectures
WalletKnowledge.subtitle: Pick a wallet to see how it is built, where its keys live, and every failure documented so far.

riskScale.title: How exposed are your funds, really?
riskScale.subtitle: Scale of risk

custodial.label: Critical
custodial.title: Custodial wallets and exchanges
custodial.body: Your keys live on a server you do not control. The platform can freeze, lose, or leak your funds — and if it fails, you are a creditor, not an owner.

hot.label: High
hot.title: Hot software wallets
hot.body: The keys sit on an online device, next to the apps you install and the links you open. Malware or a convincing page can read them before you notice.

commercial-cold.label: Caution
commercial-cold.title: Commercial cold wallets
commercial-cold.body: The keys stay offline, but the wallet runs firmware you cannot inspect, on hardware heavily exposed to supply chain risks.
commercial-cold.examples: Ledger, Trezor, Tangem, COLDCARD, and similar hardware wallets.

opensource-verifiable.label: Safe
opensource-verifiable.title: Verifiable open-source self-custody
opensource-verifiable.body: You learn to identify misleading wallet setups. You create your own secure wallet using open-source tools.

DiagramsPage.metadataDescription: Compare Blockstream Jade, Trezor and an offline Bitcoin Core wallet by the software and hardware that can see your private keys, and the action that hands them over.
DiagramsPage.title: Who reaches your private keys?
DiagramsPage.subtitle: Pick a wallet and see its whole ecosystem laid out. The highlighted elements can reach your keys at some point, and the count tells you how wide that surface is.

KeyAccessDiagram.countSummary: {count} of {total} elements can reach your keys
KeyAccessDiagram.legendAccess: Highlighted: this element sits on the path to your private keys at some point.
KeyAccessDiagram.legendNoAccess: Dashed: part of the same ecosystem, but it never holds key material.
KeyAccessDiagram.prompt: Select any element to see which of your actions opens it to the keys.
KeyAccessDiagram.actionNone: Nothing you do here hands over a key: it sees addresses, signatures or public data only.

full.label: Full keys
full.note: a readable copy of the keys exists there: the seed, or every key in the wallet file.

transient.label: In memory
transient.note: the keys are decrypted into it while it signs, then wiped.

partial.label: Partial
partial.note: it holds a passphrase or one multisig share, never the whole key.

KeyAccessDiagram.caption: Three concrete setups side by side: Jade with Blockstream Green, Trezor Safe 3 or Model T with Trezor Suite, and Bitcoin Core on an air-gapped Raspberry Pi. Every element of each ecosystem is drawn once; the highlighted ones can reach your private keys at some point, and the count above is the size of that surface. Compare the numbers before you compare the brands.

jade.name: Blockstream Jade
jade.summary: An open-source signer with a secure element. Paired with Green it only signs, and the seed stays inside the chip until you unlock it. Keep it single-sig and the Green side never sees a key.

secure-element.name: Jade secure element
secure-element.action: You type your PIN on the device: the seed lives here, and that PIN is all that separates it from plaintext.

chip.name: Jade main chip
chip.action: You approve a transaction on the device: the chip decrypts the seed into its own memory, signs, then wipes it.

green-server.name: Blockstream key server
green-server.action: You create a Protected multisig wallet in Green: Blockstream holds one of the multisig keys and co-signs every spend, though it cannot sign alone.

backup.name: Paper or steel backup
backup.action: You choose “show recovery phrase” at setup or recovery and copy the words: that paper is the key.

trezor.name: Trezor
trezor.summary: A device with a secure element, driven by Trezor Suite. The seed stays on the device, but two flows put key material on the computer: the passphrase, and recovery on older models.

secure-element.name: Trezor secure element
secure-element.action: You type your PIN on the device: the seed is stored here encrypted, and the PIN unlocks it.

chip.name: Trezor main chip
chip.action: You confirm a transaction on the touchscreen: the seed is decrypted into the chip’s memory, used to sign, then cleared.

suite.name: Trezor Suite on your computer
suite.action: You accept the default “enter passphrase on computer”: the passphrase is typed into Suite and stays in its memory.

browser.name: Suite Web or a Trezor Connect site
browser.action: You type the passphrase into a web page: the page and any extension running in it can read that field.

bridge.name: Trezor Bridge and the USB link

host-recovery.name: Host-side recovery (Model One)
host-recovery.action: You recover a wallet by typing the words into Suite: the whole seed ends up on the computer.

backup.name: Paper, steel or SLIP-39 backup
backup.action: You write the 12/24 words, or the Shamir shares, at setup: that backup is the key.

core.name: Bitcoin Core
core.model: air-gapped Raspberry Pi, PSBT over USB
core.summary: No vendor, no server: a Raspberry Pi that never joins a network holds the wallet, and you verify the Core release yourself. Every element that can reach the keys is on that board, on its card, or in your hands.

os.name: Pi OS and the Core binary
os.action: You install or update Core: whichever binary you run can read the wallet file and every key you unlock, so verify the release signature first.

memory.name: Raspberry Pi memory
memory.action: You unlock the wallet to sign a PSBT: every decrypted key sits in RAM until you lock the wallet or reboot.

keyboard.name: Keyboard, screen and shell history
keyboard.action: You type the wallet passphrase: it crosses the keyboard, the OS and the terminal in clear text.

network.name: The network (the Pi never joins one)

wallet-file.name: wallet.dat on the microSD card
wallet-file.action: You create or restore the wallet: the keys are written to this file, readable until you set an encryption passphrase.

dump.name: dumpwallet output or wallet copy
dump.action: You run dumpwallet and every private key is written in plain text, or backupwallet and the whole file leaves on a USB stick.

psbt.name: The PSBT on the USB stick

paper-passphrase.name: The passphrase you write down
paper-passphrase.action: You write the passphrase on paper so you never lose it: that paper unlocks any copy of the wallet file.
